631.quote_or_event: “The king of Ujjayinī would be my fight-guest today; yet in a matter to be settled by wit, talk of sword against sword is idle. Therefore, I shall use wit. Verily, wit is a cow of plenty for producing victory.”
631.explanation: When Pradyota besieges Rajagriha, King Shrenika turns to his son and minister Abhayakumara, who judges that this crisis calls for strategy rather than battle and picks his means to suit it.
631.tie_back: The Kural defines the minister by skill in choosing the means, the time and the method for a hard task; Abhaya's reply shows a minister weighing the situation and choosing the right instrument.
631.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10, ch. 11, part 2 ‘Contest between Pradyota and Abhaya’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
631._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (Johnson). Abhayakumara is the classic wise minister of Jain narrative; the passage shows choosing the means, but not the Kural's full list (time, method).

632.quote_or_event: “Thus I became the protector of myself and of others besides, of all living beings, whether they move or not.”
632.explanation: The monk Anathi explains to King Shrenika that by renouncing and keeping the vows he became a true protector of all beings, unlike the king with all his wealth and army.
632.tie_back: The Kural lists protecting the people among a minister's qualities, with firmness, learning and effort; the Jain verse recasts protection as the ahimsa of the self-controlled person toward all living beings.
632.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.35 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
632._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Next-best only: it touches the single quality of protecting others, and in a spiritual sense; no Jain passage found lists a minister's qualities as the Kural does.

633.quote_or_event: “All your princes have been seduced by King Śreṇika. Money has been sent them to make them his; and they, after accepting it, will bind you and deliver you to my father. The money has been buried in their dwellings for their benefit. Dig and look.”
633.explanation: Abhayakumara buries money in the camp of Pradyota's allied princes and then warns Pradyota that they have been bribed; Pradyota digs, finds the money and flees, and his allies' army breaks up.
633.tie_back: The Kural praises the minister who can split the enemy's allies away; Abhaya's stratagem does exactly that, turning Pradyota against his own princes without a battle.
633.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10, ch. 11, part 2 ‘Contest between Pradyota and Abhaya’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
633._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (Johnson). Near one-to-one on detaching the enemy's allies; the Kural's further points (keeping one's own side, winning back defectors) are not shown. Jain narrative, not doctrine.

634.quote_or_event: “He, being wise, smelled the food-bag and pronounced this decision, ‘There is here a serpent that poisons by its glance, that originated from the combination of substances. If he had opened the bag, he would have been consumed, certainly. So turn it loose in the forest with your face averted.’”
634.explanation: Held captive at Pradyota's court, Abhayakumara is asked about a messenger's food-bag; he examines it, gives a clear diagnosis and a definite instruction, and the danger is shown to be real.
634.tie_back: The Kural says a minister must study a matter, act after careful choice and state a firm conclusion; Abhaya examines the bag and gives a single, decisive verdict.
634.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10, ch. 11, part 2 ‘Contest between Pradyota and Abhaya’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
634._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (Johnson). Shows examination followed by a firm decision; it is a single anecdote of practical wisdom, not a teaching about counsel.

635.quote_or_event: “… circumspect in his speaking … guarding his thoughts, guarding his words, guarding his acts, guarding his senses, guarding his chastity; without wrath, without pride, without deceit, without greed …”
635.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra describes Mahavira as careful in speech (bhasha-samiti) and guarded in word and deed, free from the four passions.
635.tie_back: The Kural's best counsellor knows what is right and speaks with learning and restraint; the Jain ideal of careful, guarded speech free of passion covers the restraint, though not the giving of counsel.
635.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Mahavira §118 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884; sacred-texts.com)
635._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (quoted with omissions marked). Next-best only: it describes a sage's restrained speech, not an adviser's skill in counsel or knowledge of method.

636.quote_or_event: “Then the king looked with nectar-sweet glance at the face of Abhayakumāra, the depository of inborn and other kinds of knowledge …”
636.explanation: Hemacandra calls the minister Abhaya a store of 'inborn and other kinds of knowledge'; Johnson's note explains the four buddhis of Jain tradition: inborn (autpattiki), from deliberation, from training, and from past karma.
636.tie_back: The Kural says no scheme can outwit one who joins native sharpness with learning; the Jain portrait of Abhaya, who has both inborn intelligence and acquired kinds, is the minister the schemes of Pradyota failed against.
636.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10, ch. 11, part 2 ‘Contest between Pradyota and Abhaya’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
636._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (Johnson); the four-buddhi list is in Johnson's footnote, paraphrased here. Good fit on inborn plus acquired intelligence, though Abhaya is in fact tricked once in the same episode.

637.quote_or_event: “You, although knowing nīti and well versed in the seventy stories, were caught by her like a parrot by a cat.”
637.explanation: Pradyota taunts Abhayakumara, who was captured when a courtesan posing as a pious Jain laywoman drugged him: all his learning in statecraft (niti) did not protect him from a trick of the world.
637.tie_back: The Kural warns that knowing methods from books is not enough without knowing how the world actually behaves; Abhaya's capture is a cautionary case of learned policy failing against real-world deceit.
637.source: Hemacandra, Triṣaṣṭiśalākāpuruṣacaritra, Book 10, ch. 11, part 2 ‘Contest between Pradyota and Abhaya’ (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
637._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org (Johnson). A negative example rather than a teaching, and spoken by a hostile king, but it fits the Kural's warning closely.

638.quote_or_event: “If you have no intention of abandoning pleasure, and still long for undertakings and property, my long talk has been to no purpose. I go, king, farewell.” And Brahmadatta, king of the Pañkâlas, did not act on the counsel of the saint …
638.explanation: The monk Citta, out of old friendship and concern for the king's welfare, gives the emperor Brahmadatta honest advice again and again; the king admits he knows the Law but will not follow it, and comes to ruin.
638.tie_back: The Kural says that even when the king rejects good counsel and is ignorant himself, the one beside him must still tell him what is truly good; Citta does this to the end, though the king will not listen.
638.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 13.33-34 (cf. 13.15) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
638._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (Jacobi's 'Pa*ñ**k*âlas' rendered Pañkâlas). Strong fit on giving good counsel to an unwilling king; Citta is a monk and former brother, not a minister, and in the end he leaves.

639.quote_or_event: “A cut-throat enemy will not do him such harm as his own perversity will do him; the man without pity will feel repentance in the hour of death.”
639.explanation: The monk Anathi warns that harm from within, a person's own wrong conduct, is worse than anything an outside enemy can do.
639.tie_back: The Kural judges one treacherous minister at your side worse than seventy crores of open foes; the Jain verse makes the same comparison of an inner enemy with an outer one, though the inner enemy is one's own perversity.
639.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.48 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
639._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The structure (an inner foe worse than an outer one) matches, but the Jain inner foe is one's own soul's misconduct, not a treacherous adviser.

640.quote_or_event: “Just as bad bullocks are when put before a car, so are bad pupils when yoked, as it were, to the car of the Law; they break down through want of zeal.”
640.explanation: The teacher Garga compares bad pupils to unruly bullocks that break down on the road, failing to carry through what they were set to do.
640.tie_back: The Kural says those who lack the ability to carry things through leave their work unfinished even after proper planning; Garga's bullocks and pupils likewise break down short of the goal for lack of zeal.
640.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 27.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
640._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Next-best: it concerns failing to finish from lack of zeal, but nothing about prior planning or ministers.
